column2: those passionless, perfected ascetics, full of vigour and rich in austerity. Subtle, cool, fragrant and pleasant to the touch, O brahmins,
the best of the seven winds, which goes to the auspicious worlds, carries them, O best of brahmins, to the highest goal of the sky.
The sky carries these lords of the world to the highest goal of rajas; rajas carries them, O best of brahmins, to the highest goal of sattva;
sattva, pure in nature, carries them to the supreme lord Narayana; and the Lord, pure in nature, of himself carries them to the Supreme Self.
Reaching the Supreme Self and becoming one with it, the stainless ascetics become fit for immortality and do not return, O brahmins.
That is the highest goal, O brahmins, of the great-souled ones free from the pairs of opposites, devoted to truth and straightforwardness and compassionate to all beings.

Reaching that highest state, the Blessed One, those firm in their vows — do they delight there until the end of birth and death, or not?
brahmapuran:240:78	Please tell us truly what the fact is here; there is no other man but you whom we may ask, O good one.
brahmapuran:240:79	This is a great flaw in liberation, if the ascetics who have attained perfection remain in that very knowledge.
brahmapuran:240:80	We see the dharma marked by activity as supreme, O brahmin; for one sunk in the highest knowledge, might there not be yet another sorrow?

Fittingly, best of sages, have you asked a difficult question; even the wise are bewildered by this question, O best of sages.
brahmapuran:240:82	Hear my words on this too, the supreme truth, where the highest understanding of the great-souled followers of Kapila lies.
brahmapuran:240:83	The senses of embodied beings perceive their own body, O brahmins; they are the instruments of the Self, and through them he sees what is subtle.
brahmapuran:240:84	Deprived of the Self, they are like wood or a wall, and perish without doubt, like waves on the great ocean.
brahmapuran:240:85	When the embodied one sleeps with his senses, O best of brahmins, the subtle one moves everywhere, like wind in the sky.
brahmapuran:240:86	He sees fittingly, remembers and touches, sinless ones, understanding everything here as before, O brahmins.
brahmapuran:240:87	All the senses, each in its own place as ordained, dissolve for lack of mastery, like snakes whose poison is spent.
brahmapuran:240:88	Overpowering the subtle movements of all the senses in their own places, the Self moves on, without doubt.
brahmapuran:240:89	All the qualities of sattva, the qualities of rajas, all the qualities of tamas and the qualities of the intellect, O good ones,
brahmapuran:240:90	the qualities of the mind and of space, the qualities of wind, O all-knowing ones, and the qualities born of moisture,
brahmapuran:240:91	the qualities of water, O brahmins, and the qualities of earth — pervading all with these qualities in the knowers of the field, O best of brahmins,
brahmapuran:240:92	the Self, the knower of the field, moves through good and bad by karma; and the senses follow that great Self like disciples, O brahmins.
brahmapuran:240:93	Passing beyond Prakriti, he reaches the pure, subtle, higher than the high — Narayana, the great Self, changeless, higher than the high,
brahmapuran:240:94	freed from all sins, entering the one free from ill, the Supreme Self without qualities, at rest, O good ones.
brahmapuran:240:95	There the best mind and the senses, O brahmins, come in due time, carrying out the teacher's command.
brahmapuran:240:96	It is possible in a short time to attain peace and those qualities; so by this Sankhya-yoga that has been described, O best of brahmins, one reaches liberation.
brahmapuran:240:97	The Sankhya brahmins, deeply wise, reach the highest goal by this knowledge, O best of brahmins; there is no knowledge equal to it.
brahmapuran:240:98	Have no doubt here: Sankhya knowledge is held to be supreme. The imperishable and constant, the eternal Brahman, was spoken of before —
brahmapuran:240:99	without beginning, middle or end, beyond the pairs, the agent, everlasting, unchanging and eternal, as the tranquil ones describe it,
brahmapuran:240:100	from which all the changes of creation and dissolution proceed. So do the great sages who teach declare in the scriptures.
brahmapuran:240:101	All brahmins and the Vedas, and those who know the Sama, the supreme god devoted to Brahman, the infinite and supremely imperishable one,
brahmapuran:240:102	seeking him, O brahmins, speak of him with minds bound to qualities. The yogas have been rightly taught, and the Sankhyas of boundless insight.
brahmapuran:240:103	His formless aspect, O best of brahmins, is Sankhya, and his form, says scripture; the great ones call these his signs, O best of sages.
brahmapuran:240:104	Beings on earth are of two kinds, O best of brahmins, called the unreachable and the reachable, and of these the reachable is superior.
brahmapuran:240:105	The great knowledge of the great one, O brahmins, found in the Vedas, in Sankhya and in yoga, and what is duly seen in the Puranas — all that has come from Sankhya, O lords of sages.
brahmapuran:240:106	What is seen in the great histories, what is specially seen in the true treatises, and whatever knowledge there is in the world here — that too has come from Sankhya, O great lords of sages.
brahmapuran:240:107	The supreme power seen by all, knowledge and liberation have been duly declared, and the subtle austerities too have been duly set out in Sankhya, O brahmins.
brahmapuran:240:108	The Sankhyas always reach the reverse of that, which is their good, constantly and with ease; and having held on to these, their purpose accomplished, they come down again into the homes of brahmins.
brahmapuran:240:109	Abandoning the body, the yogis and Sankhyas enter liberation, and some become dwellers of heaven; so all the more should you delight here, O brahmins, in the precious Sankhya cherished by the good.
brahmapuran:240:110	For them no going among animals is seen, no downward course, no abode of evildoers; nor are those twice-born who are not attached to this knowledge, O sages, truly foremost.
brahmapuran:240:111	Sankhya is vast, supreme and ancient, a great ocean, stainless and nobly beautiful; the Sankhya sages, O great one, place it wholly and immeasurably in Narayana.
brahmapuran:240:112	This I have told as the supreme truth: from Narayana comes this ancient universe; at the time of creation he makes creation, and at the time of dissolution he withdraws it again.
brahmapuran:241:15	Minuteness, lightness, attainment, lordship, the imperishable light, with hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads and faces everywhere,
brahmapuran:241:16	with ears everywhere in the world, it stands enveloping all. This blessed Hiranyagarbha is called Buddhi in tradition,
brahmapuran:241:17	Mahat in the yoga texts and Viranchi as well, and in the Sankhya scripture he is recited by many names, manifold in nature.
brahmapuran:241:18	Of varied form, the Self of the universe, he is known as the One Imperishable, by whom the whole three worlds, one in nature, are upheld by himself.
brahmapuran:241:19	Likewise, because of his many forms he is known as Vishvarupa. Undergoing change, he creates himself by himself.
brahmapuran:241:20	From his union with Pradhana the vast city arises; the greatly radiant one produces ahamkara, saluted by Prajapati.
brahmapuran:241:21	What passes from the unmanifest to the manifest they call the creation of knowledge; and Mahat and ahamkara are the creation of ignorance.
brahmapuran:241:22	The unmoving and the moving arose likewise from one source; those who reflect on scripture know them as knowledge and ignorance.
brahmapuran:241:23	Know the creation of the elements from ahamkara as the third, O king; and in the ahamkaras, O lord of men, know the fourth, the modified creation:
brahmapuran:241:24	wind, fire, space, water and earth, and sound, touch, form, taste and smell.
brahmapuran:241:25	Thus the group of ten arose at once, without doubt. Know the fifth, O king of kings, as the elemental creation that serves purposes:
brahmapuran:241:26	ear, skin, eyes, tongue and nose as the fifth, speech, hands, feet, anus and generative organ —
brahmapuran:241:27	these senses of knowledge and senses of action arose here together with the mind, O king.
brahmapuran:241:28	This is the set of twenty-four principles, from which all forms proceed; knowing it, brahmins who see the truth do not grieve.
brahmapuran:241:29	Thus has this excellent threefold world arisen; it should always be known, O best of men, in the ocean of hell,
brahmapuran:241:30	with Yakshas, ghosts and Gandharvas, with Kinnaras and great serpents, with Charanas and Pishachas, with divine sages and night-roamers,
brahmapuran:241:31	with gadflies, worms and mosquitoes, with putrid maggots and rats, in the dog, the dog-cooker, the antelope, the Chandala and the Pulkasa,
brahmapuran:241:32	in the elephant, horse, donkey, tiger, wolf and cow — whatever form there is, anything at all, everywhere this is the illustration.
brahmapuran:241:33	In water, on land and in the sky, and nowhere else — this is certain — was the dwelling of embodied beings; so we have heard.
brahmapuran:241:34	All of this, dear one, what is called manifest, wastes away day after day; the Self of beings is what is called the imperishable.
brahmapuran:241:35	Therefore that is called perishable (kshara), since this world wastes away; and they call the world, which springs from the unmanifest and is called manifest, deluding in nature.
brahmapuran:241:36	Mahat and the imperishable are eternal; this is free from perishing. I have told you, great king, that from which there is no return.
brahmapuran:241:37	The twenty-fifth is formless, eternal, called the Principle; because it rests in sattva, the wise call the principle sattva.
brahmapuran:241:38	That which, formless, created the manifest, presides over form; the manifest is the twenty-fourth, and the formless is the twenty-fifth.
brahmapuran:241:39	He, self-possessed, dwells in the heart of all forms, conscious and making conscious, eternal, of every form yet formless.
brahmapuran:241:40	By the law of creation and dissolution he is of the nature of creation and dissolution; he always abides in the realm of the senses, without qualities yet called by qualities.
brahmapuran:241:41	Thus this great Self, undergoing change through countless creations and dissolutions and joined with Prakriti, should not, if wise, identify with it.
brahmapuran:241:42	Joined with tamas, sattva and rajas, he is absorbed in those various wombs here, through lack of awakening and through keeping company with the unawakened.
brahmapuran:241:43	Through living together he thinks, I am a child"; told "What I am, I am not," he simply follows the qualities.
Through tamas he comes to various tamasic states, through rajas to rajasic ones, and to sattvic ones through resorting to sattva.
White, red and black are these three forms; know all these forms to be of Prakriti.
The tamasic go to hell, the rajasic to human birth, and the sattvic, sharing in happiness, go to the world of the gods.
By sin alone one is born among animals; by merit and sin mixed, as a human; and by merit alone, among the gods.
Thus the wise say that liberation lies beyond the unmanifest; it comes about for the twenty-fifth through knowledge alone.
Living on cow's urine, eating kasha flowers, eating moss, or living by some other means,
living on withered leaves and eating scattered fruits, he undertakes various penances in the hope of success,
the chandrayana fasts performed duly, various outward marks, the practices tied to the four stages of life, and those resting on dharma and adharma,
other refuges and various heretical sects, secluded rock shelters and springs,
solitary sandbanks and various forests, secluded places in the woods and the great caves of mountains,
various disciplines and austerities, sacrifices of many kinds and various branches of learning,
the path of trade, brahmins, kshatriyas, vaishyas and shudras, and gifts of many kinds to the poor, the blind, the wretched and others —
he imagines he is taking these up, and likewise the various qualities, sattva, rajas and tamas, dharma, wealth and pleasure.
Thus the Self divides itself as Prakriti. The cries of svaha and vashat, the cry of svadha and the act of salutation,
sacrificing and studying, giving and likewise receiving, officiating at sacrifices and teaching, and whatever else there is,
through the ordering of birth and death, and through slaughter — all this fear of good and bad they call eternal.
The goddess Prakriti creates fear and dissolution; at the end of the day he alone remains, having passed beyond these qualities.
As the sun draws in its net of rays at that time, so he regards all this as play —
these various qualities of his own form, dear to the heart. Thus producing this activity whose nature is creation and dissolution,
attached to the path of action, of three qualities and lord of the three qualities, following the path of action and inaction, he thinks, 'That is so.'
By Prakriti this whole world has been made blind, O lord, pervaded in many ways by rajas and tamas.
'So the pairs of opposites that have passed always turn upon me; from me they arise and in dissolution they go back to me.
All these must be crossed,' O king, so he thinks, out of partial understanding; and so too of his good deeds:
'These are to be enjoyed by me when I have gone to the world of the gods; and here too I shall enjoy the rising fruit of good and bad.
Happiness must be made thus; having once made my happiness, my happiness will last birth after birth;
and by what I have done here there will be endless freedom from sorrow for me.' Human life is pleasure and pain, and there is sinking into hell as well.
'From hell I shall come again in time to human birth, from human birth to godhood, and from godhood again to manhood;
and from manhood he goes to hell in turn.' Such is the self of the twice-born, enveloped by the qualities;
by it he comes to gods, men and hell; always wrapped in the sense of 'mine,' he turns about right there
through thousands of crores of creations, in forms that end in death. He who performs karma that bears good and bad fruit in this way
obtains the fruit thus, embodied in the three worlds. Prakriti performs the karma bearing good and bad fruit,
and Prakriti, going where it will, likewise obtains it in the three worlds — in animal birth, in human birth and in the world of the gods.
These three states should be known as belonging to Prakriti. Because Prakriti is without marks, it is inferred through its marks;
and likewise the mark of the Purusha is known by inference. Entering another body, the flawless body of Prakriti,
and occupying the openings of its wounds, he thinks of actions as belonging to himself. The ear and the rest, and the five senses of action,
and passion and the like operate here among the qualities along with the qualities. 'I am doing these; these senses are mine' —
so, though without senses, he thinks; though without wounds, he thinks 'I am wounded'; though without marks, he thinks himself marked; though beyond time, he thinks himself subject to time;
though without sattva, he thinks himself sattva; though immortal, he thinks himself dead; though deathless, he thinks himself death; though unmoving, he thinks himself moving;
though without a field, he thinks himself the field; though unattached, attached; though not a principle, a principle; though unborn, born;
though imperishable, he thinks himself perishable, through lack of understanding. Thus through lack of awakening and keeping company with the unawakened,
he goes through thousands of crores of creations ending in a fall, and through thousands of births ending in death,
in animal birth, human birth and the world of the gods, like the moon through its phases, again there by the thousand.
So the ill-minded one is led on through lack of awakening. The fifteenth digit is the source; that is said to be its abode.
Know that the moon always has sixteen parts; through a digit the unwise one is born again and again continually.
The wise one is not born thus, O king. The sixteenth digit is subtle; understand that to be the true Soma.
It is not consumed by the gods, but it nourishes the gods. Having destroyed the sense of 'mine,' O best of kings, he is born; for Prakriti has three qualities, and he becomes of three qualities too.
Prakriti, without marks, is perceived through the marks born of itself, as the embodied and the formless are always perceived through flowers and fruits.
So too by inference the mark is perceived; the twenty-fifth, dear one, is fixed in nature among the marks,
without beginning or end, infinite, the sole seer of all; only because of identification is it called a quality among the qualities.
Qualities belong to what has qualities; how can what is without qualities have them? So those who see the qualities understand.
But when he identifies with these qualities of Prakriti, then he becomes possessed of qualities and sees the distinctions of qualities.
That which they call beyond the intellect, and Sankhya-yoga in every way, the deeply wise call the awakening one, through setting aside the awakened.
They call the Lord unawakened as manifested by his own qualities, and the Lord without qualities eternal, the presiding one.
The twenty-fifth, beyond Prakriti and the qualities, the wise who are skilled in Sankhya-yoga and seek the supreme understand.
When the unmanifest is awakened, and the states are silent, they do not know the awakening one; then they understand it as the same.
This is a proper illustration, not a proper vision; they understand the awakening one as distinct from the two, O subduer of foes.
This illustration of the perishable and imperishable has been stated in relation to each other: oneness they call the imperishable, and multiplicity is called the perishable.
When he is established in the twenty-fifth, then they speak rightly; his vision of oneness and his vision of multiplicity —
the knower of principles sees this illustration of the two principles as distinct. The wise call the principle with the twenty-five principles 'the principle';
the wise call what is beyond the twenty-fifth free of principles. The conduct to be avoided is the avoidance of what is to be avoided; the eternal principle is beyond the principle."

You have spoken of multiplicity and oneness, O best of brahmins, but to one who looks, the illustration of these two remains doubtful.
brahmapuran:243:42	Likewise, sinless one, with my gross understanding I cannot see the truth of the awakened, the unawakened and the awakening one; there is no doubt of this.
brahmapuran:243:43	And the reason you gave for the imperishable and the perishable seems lost to me, sinless one, because my understanding is unsteady.
brahmapuran:243:44	So I wish to hear this: the vision of multiplicity and oneness, the pair and the unobstructed, and the awakening one, in truth;
brahmapuran:243:45	knowledge and ignorance, blessed one, the imperishable and the perishable, and Sankhya-yoga fully, the awakened and the unawakened, each separately.

Well then, I will tell you what you ask. Hear from me separately, great king, the practice of yoga.
brahmapuran:243:47	The practice of the yogas is meditation, which is their supreme strength; and that meditation, those who know say, is twofold:
brahmapuran:243:48	one-pointedness of mind and breath control; and breath control is with qualities, while the mental one is without qualities.
brahmapuran:243:49	At the times of passing urine and stool and of eating, O king, one should not practise; at the other times one should practise intently.
brahmapuran:243:50	The sage, withdrawing the senses from their objects with the mind, with ten or twelve (breath-controls), for he is beyond the twenty-four,
brahmapuran:243:51	and the wise one should not urge himself with urgings; that unageing one who abides is what the wise have spoken of.
brahmapuran:243:52	The Self of the universe is always to be known — so we have heard. It is the object for one whose mind is not deficient; not otherwise — this is certain.
brahmapuran:243:53	Freed from all attachments, eating lightly, with senses conquered, in the early part of the night and the latter one should hold the mind in the heart.
brahmapuran:243:54	Making the group of senses steady by the mind, O lord of Mithila, and the mind steady by the intellect, motionless as a stone,
brahmapuran:243:55	one should be unshakable as a post and motionless as a log. The one who knows the rules of practice through the intellect is then called 'yoked.'
brahmapuran:243:56	He does not hear, smell or see anything; he does not perceive touch, and his mind forms no intentions;
brahmapuran:243:57	he does not think of anything and is not aware, like a log; then the wise call him yoked, having reached his true nature.
brahmapuran:243:58	As a lamp in a windless place does not flicker, so his radiance is seen; free from marks, he may move below, above and across.
brahmapuran:243:59	Then, having attained that, he is said to be the one in whom it is seen: the inner Self dwelling in the heart is to be known as the knower by such as me, dear one.
brahmapuran:243:60	Like a smokeless fire, like the sun with its rays, like lightning's fire in the sky, he sees the Self in the self.
brahmapuran:243:61	Great-souled, steadfast and wise brahmins, established in the source of Brahman, behold him, the sourceless and immortal.
brahmapuran:243:62	They call it subtler than the subtlest and greater than the greatest; everywhere in all beings it abides unmoving, yet is not seen.
brahmapuran:243:63	By the visible substance of the intellect and the lamp of the mind the maker of the world is seen; standing beyond the great darkness, dear one, he is not of darkness.
brahmapuran:243:64	Those who know the truth and have mastered the Vedas call him 'far from darkness,' stainless, beyond opinion, without marks, called the markless.
brahmapuran:243:65	This is the yoga of the worlds; what other mark of yoga is there? Seeing thus, one beholds the unageing, supreme Self.
brahmapuran:243:66	This much I have told you truly of the vision of yoga; now I will tell of Sankhya knowledge, the illustration of enumeration.
brahmapuran:243:67	The unmanifest they call the first, the supreme Prakriti of the Self; from it Mahat arose as the second, O best of kings.
brahmapuran:243:68	Ahamkara from Mahat is the third, so we have heard; from ahamkara come the five elements, say those who see the Self through Sankhya.
brahmapuran:243:69	These are the eight Prakritis, and the modifications are sixteen: the five particulars and the five senses, and so on.
brahmapuran:243:70	This much the wise call the Sankhya of the principles; those who know the Sankhya rules abide ever on the Sankhya path.
brahmapuran:243:71	Whatever arises from something dissolves back into it; they dissolve in reverse order and are taken up by the inner Self.
brahmapuran:243:72	They arise in forward order and dissolve in reverse order — qualities into qualities, continually, like the waves of the ocean.
brahmapuran:243:73	Such is the creation and dissolution of Prakriti, O best of kings: oneness in dissolution and multiplicity in creation.
brahmapuran:243:74	So it should be understood by those skilled in knowledge, O king of kings; and this is also the illustration of its presiding unmanifest one.
brahmapuran:243:75	The knower of principles follows the oneness and multiplicity of Prakriti: its oneness in dissolution and its multiplicity from its unfolding.
brahmapuran:243:76	The manifold Self produces Prakriti, whose nature is to bring forth, and the great Self, the twenty-fifth, presides over that field.
brahmapuran:243:77	He is called the presiding one by the best of ascetics, O king of kings; the presider over the fields because of his presiding, so we have heard.
brahmapuran:243:78	He knows the field, the unmanifest, and so is called the knower of the field; he lies in the unmanifest city and so is called Purusha.
brahmapuran:243:79	The field is one thing and the knower of the field is said to be another; the field is called the unmanifest, and the knower is the twenty-fifth.
brahmapuran:243:80	Knowledge is one thing and the knowable is said to be another; knowledge is called the unmanifest, and the knowable is the twenty-fifth.
brahmapuran:243:81	The unmanifest is called the field, and likewise sattva and the lord; the twenty-fifth is not a lord and not a principle, yet it is the principle.

brahmapuran:243:83	Enumerating truly the twenty-four and the forty, and counting a thousand times, the twenty-fifth is free of principles.
brahmapuran:243:84	The twenty-fifth, whose self is awakened, is known as the awakening one; when he awakens to the Self, then he becomes alone (kevala).
brahmapuran:243:85	This much I have told you truly of right vision; those who understand it thus attain sameness.
brahmapuran:243:86	Right illustration is direct perception of Prakriti; just as these arise from what has qualities, so it would be from the qualityless.
brahmapuran:243:87	For those who abide thus there is no returning again; the perishable state exists, but not the mutual imperishable.
brahmapuran:243:88	Those of poor understanding who do not see rightly, and whose vision rests on these, come to manifestation again and again, O subduer of foes.
brahmapuran:243:89	Those who know all this, but not through awakening to the whole, will become manifest beings because they follow only the manifest.
brahmapuran:243:90	All is said to be unmanifest, and the twenty-fifth is not all; those who understand this have no fear.
brahmapuran:244:14	The qualities beginning with Mahat arise from one another; the presiding field they call this twenty-fifth.
brahmapuran:244:15	The net of qualities within should be drawn into the manifest self; then that 'I' with those qualities dissolves into the twenty-fifth.

brahmapuran:244:19	He becomes perishable when Prakriti with qualities is among the qualities; but then he knows Prakriti, and likewise his own qualitylessness.

brahmapuran:244:23	'What have I done all this time, sinking in time? Like a fish that, through knowing nothing else, followed the water,
brahmapuran:244:24	I myself, out of delusion, went from one person to another, from birth to birth, as a fish followed the water here through its knowledge of water.
brahmapuran:244:25	The fish, out of ignorance, does not think itself other than the water; and I, through disregard, do not know the Self as other.
brahmapuran:244:26	Fie on me, ill-minded one, who, sunk in this, followed again out of delusion from one person to another, from birth to birth.
brahmapuran:244:27	This one may be my kinsman; with him I meet decline. I have reached sameness and oneness: as he is, so am I.
brahmapuran:244:28	I see equality here; I am truly like him. He is plainly stainless, and I am such as he.
brahmapuran:244:29	I, who out of the delusion of ignorance acted with the ignorant one, through association and excessive association, have stayed all this time.
brahmapuran:244:30	I, so subjugated, did not recognize this time. How shall I dwell with her who is of high, low and middle kinds?
brahmapuran:244:31	How can I live with one of like illusion here? Out of lack of understanding I went; now be steady here.
brahmapuran:244:32	I will not live with her any longer, having been deceived all this time; for I, changeless, was deceived by her who is change.
brahmapuran:244:33	That was not her fault; the fault is mine, for I became attached here, having turned my face away.
brahmapuran:244:34	So I stayed in this of many forms, embodied though formless; and the formless, of formless nature, was overpowered by the sense of 'mine.'
brahmapuran:244:35	By that Prakriti, in those various wombs here, I who am without 'mine' was altered by the sense of 'mine' in each of them,
brahmapuran:244:36	dwelling in wombs with a mind whose awareness was lost. I made no equality with her in the ego.
brahmapuran:244:37	Having made the self manifold, she joins me again; now I am awakened, free of 'mine' and free of ego.
brahmapuran:244:38	Abandoning the sense of 'mine,' always made by the mind and shaped by ego, and abandoning her who clung to me, I will resort to the one free from ill.
brahmapuran:244:39	With him I will attain sameness, not with this unconscious one; my welfare lies with him, not in oneness with her.'
brahmapuran:244:40	Thus through supreme awakening the twenty-fifth is awakened; abandoning the perishable, he attains the imperishable, free from ill.
brahmapuran:244:41	The unmanifest with the qualities of the manifest, with qualities and without — having first seen the qualityless, one becomes like it, O king of Mithila.
brahmapuran:244:42	This illustration of the imperishable and the perishable I have given you here, full of knowledge, as shown by scripture.
brahmapuran:244:43	Free from doubt, subtle, pure and stainless — I will tell it to you again; learn it as it has been heard.
brahmapuran:244:44	I have taught Sankhya-yoga through the illustration of the two scriptures; what is taught in the Sankhya scripture is itself the vision of yoga.
brahmapuran:244:45	The knowledge of the Sankhyas aimed at awakening, O lord of the earth, is set out clearly there for the good of disciples.
brahmapuran:244:46	The learned call this scripture vast; and in this scripture, for the yogas, with rebirth in view,
brahmapuran:244:47	a principle beyond the twenty-fifth is recited, O king; but for the Sankhyas the supreme principle has been described as it is.
brahmapuran:244:48	The awakened, the unawakened and the awakening one in truth; the awakening one and awakenedness they call the vision of yoga.
brahmapuran:245:39	This is unfathomable, unageing and immortal, free from ill, free from fear and auspicious; having examined the delusion called the doctrine of others and understood this, the meaning of its truth —
brahmapuran:245:40	this was obtained of old from the eternal Hiranyagarbha, O king, by carefully pleasing that fiercely radiant, eternal Brahman, just as you have received it from me.
brahmapuran:245:41	As you asked me, O king, so have I told it to you, and nothing else; as I obtained from Brahma, O king, this great knowledge, the final refuge of those who know liberation.
brahmapuran:245:42	This is declared the Supreme Brahman, from which there is no return — the twenty-fifth, best of sages, as Vasishtha told it long ago.
brahmapuran:245:43	One returns again who does not truly understand the supreme, imperishable knowledge, the unageing and immortal awakening one.
brahmapuran:245:44	This supreme knowledge that brings the highest good I have told you truly, O brahmins, as heard from the divine sage.
brahmapuran:245:45	It was received from Hiranyagarbha by the sage Vasishtha; from Vasishtha, Narada, tiger among sages, obtained it;
brahmapuran:245:46	from Narada I learned it, and I have told you this eternal teaching. Grieve not, best of sages, having heard of this supreme state.
brahmapuran:245:47	He who distinguishes the perishable from the imperishable has no fear; fear is for him who does not know this truly.
brahmapuran:245:48	Through lack of understanding the deluded one meets with misfortunes again and again, and after death undergoes thousands of births ending in death.
brahmapuran:245:49	He attains the world of the gods, or animal or human birth, or perhaps he is released from that ocean of ignorance.
brahmapuran:245:50	In the terrible ocean of ignorance, called the unfathomable unmanifest, beings sink day after day, O brahmins.
brahmapuran:245:51	From that unfathomable, eternal unmanifest, when it wanes — therefore, O brahmins, become free of rajas and free of tamas.
brahmapuran:245:52	Thus, best of sages, I have told you the supreme liberation, the essence of essences, knowing which one does not return.
brahmapuran:245:53	It should never be given to an unbeliever, nor to one without devotion, nor to one of wicked mind, O brahmins, nor to one averse to faith.
brahmapuran:246:12	The eyes of those blinded by the darkness of ignorance and led astray by false views have been opened by you with the salve-stick of knowledge."
Having said this and honoured Vyasa, and having been honoured by him, they all went back, their purpose fulfilled, to their own hermitages as they had come.
So, best of sages, I have told this eternal Purana, most holy and destroying all sins.
As you asked me the question, O best of brahmins, by the grace of Vyasa I have recounted it all.
It should be heard by householders, ascetics and celibate students; it gives men wealth and happiness, and is purifying and destroys sin.
Likewise it should be heard with great care by brahmins devoted to Brahman and by brahmins and others who are self-controlled and seek the highest good.
A brahmin gains learning, a kshatriya victory in battle, a vaishya inexhaustible wealth, and a shudra happiness.
Whatever desire a pure man holds in mind while hearing it, that desire he obtains; there is no doubt of this.
This Vaishnava Purana destroys all sin, excels all scriptures, and brings about the aims of human life.
This Purana I have told you is equal to the Veda; when it is heard, the mass of sin arising from all faults is destroyed.
What a man gains by fasting at Prayaga, Pushkara, Kurukshetra and Arbuda, he gains by hearing this.
The fruit of great merit, O brahmins, that one does not obtain even by a year of well-offered agnihotra, one obtains by hearing this once.
The fruit a man gains by bathing in the Yamuna on the twelfth of the bright half of Jyeshtha and seeing Hari at Mathura,
he gains fully by reciting this Purana with concentration, O brahmins, his mind offered to Keshava.
Whatever fruit a man gains by beholding the rite, that fruit he obtains who reads or hears this.
The mortal who daily reads or hears with faith this Purana equal to the Veda goes to the world of Hari.
The brahmin who, self-controlled, always recites it on the festival days and on the eleventh and twelfth lunar days goes to Vishnu's world.
It brings men fame, long life, happiness, increasing renown, strength and nourishment; it is blessed and destroys bad dreams.
The learned man who reads this excellent narrative with faith and full concentration at the three junctions of the day obtains all he desires.
The sick is freed from sickness, the bound from bondage, the frightened from fear, and the one in distress from distress.
A man gains memory of past births, learning, sons, intelligence, cattle, steadfastness, dharma, wealth, pleasure and liberation.
Whatever desires a man has in mind when he reads it with a restrained mind, all of them he obtains; there is no doubt.

The man who always hears this, which grants heaven and final release, bowing to Vishnu, teacher of the world and giver of boons, with single-minded devotion and purity, enjoys happiness here, freed from stain, and divine happiness in heaven, and afterwards goes to Hari's stainless abode, freed from the qualities of Prakriti.

So this excellent text, rich in fruit, granting dharma, wealth and liberation, should be heard by the best of brahmins devoted to their own dharma who seek the one path to liberation, by self-restrained bulls among kshatriyas always seeking the good, by vaishyas daily, and by righteous shudras born of pure families.

May your mind be set on dharma, you best of men; for dharma alone is the friend of one who has gone to the next world. Wealth and women, though served even by the skilful, gain neither lasting power nor stability.
By dharma a man gains a kingdom, by dharma a man goes to heaven; long life, fame, austerity and dharma — by dharma a man gains liberation.
Dharma is a man's mother and father here, dharma his friend here and in the next world; dharma is the protector here and the giver of liberation; without dharma there is nothing at all.
This secret and excellent Purana, equal to the Veda, should not be given to one of wicked mind, and especially not to an unbeliever.
This excellent Purana I have told, which removes sin and increases dharma; you have heard this supreme secret. Give me leave, O sages; I depart.
Even beyond the gifts given at those places is this one; those gifts do not equal a sixteenth part of this gift of a bed.
Wherever that being is born, there he enjoys its fruit; when his karma is spent he comes to earth as a man of pleasing appearance,
very wealthy, knowing dharma and skilled in all the scriptures; and when that best of men dies, he goes again to Vaikuntha.
Mounting a celestial car, surrounded by Apsaras, he rejoices with the ancestors in the offerings to gods and ancestors.
The shraddha performed on the Ashtaka days and on the new-moon day, under the Magha constellation, and on whatever days are sacred to the ancestors —
hear, Tarkshya, as is proper: if the ancestors are in the state of ghosts, the shraddhas do not reach them without the sapindikarana rite.
The sapindikarana must be performed when the year is complete, without doubt; having first performed the sixteen rites for the purification of the corpse,
one should perform it for the purification of the line of ancestors; and on an occasion of prosperity one may perform it earlier; for a shudra, at his own discretion.

Now, for one who keeps the sacred fires, the sapindana should be done on the twelfth day; until he does it he remains a ghost though a fire-keeper. So for the fire-keeper the sapindana should be done on the twelfth day.
The rite for the bones, the shraddha at Gaya and the shraddha of the dark fortnight should not be performed within the year without the sapindikarana.
If there are many co-wives and one has a son, all of them become mothers of sons through that one son.
A son who keeps the fire should not perform the ancestral sacrifice without the sapindikarana; by doing so he becomes a sinner and even a slayer of his father.
The woman who gives up her life when her husband dies should have her sapindana performed together with her husband.
For a wife married in any way — a vaishya or a kshatriya — whoever are the wives of the father, some son should perform the sapindana.
When a shudra woman has been married by a brahmin through negligence, the shraddha for her is the ekoddishta, and she is joined only with him.
The other ten kinds of sons born in the four classes should always be joined with their respective mothers in the sapindikarana.
In the shraddha on the Anvashtaka days and in the shraddha for prosperity, the rice-ball for the father should be given separately, and for a woman in her sapindana.
The mother should be united with the grandmother and the father with the grandfathers in the sapindikarana — this, Tarkshya, is my view.
When a woman without sons dies, her husband should perform the sapindana, joining her with the three beginning with the mother according to dharma.
If a woman has neither son nor husband, Tarkshya, her sapindana should be performed at a time of prosperity by her brother, an heir or her brother-in-law.
For women without husband or son, and without any kinsman or brother-in-law, it should be given by the ekoddishta rite by someone else along with the brothers.
If the sapindana has not been done through ignorance or some obstacle, then the nine, the sixteen shraddhas and the annual rite should be performed.
Where there has been no cremation it should not be performed; the wise should have it done after cremation. Making an effigy of darbha grass, one should burn it with fire as the corpse.
It is to be done for the father by the son; the father should not do it for the son. Out of excessive affection one should not perform the sapindikarana for a son.
Even when there are many sons, only one should perform the rite: the nine shraddhas, the sapindana and the other sixteen shraddhas
are to be done by one alone, even when the wealth is undivided; one alone performs the last rites, as the sages have declared.
But when the sons have divided the property, the annual and other rites should be performed separately, each son doing it himself.
For one for whom these sixteen shraddhas for the departed have not been given, the state of a pishacha is fixed, even if hundreds of shraddhas are performed.
A brother, a brother's son, a sapinda kinsman or a disciple should perform the sapindikarana for one who has no son, O lord of birds.
For all who have no sons the wife should perform the sapindana, or else have it done by an officiating priest or the family priest.
If an eclipse occurs within the year after the father's death, the sons should not perform the parvana shraddha, nor the nandimukha shraddha.
The tirtha shraddha, the Gaya shraddha and other ancestral shraddhas should not be performed within the year after the death of a great elder.
On a Yamaka day, in the Gajacchaya, on the Manvadi and Yugadi days, the rice-ball for the ancestors should not be given without the sapindikarana.
Some say that the gift to the Person of Sacrifice and to the gods and others should be made even within the incomplete year.
And whatever is given to the ancestors without the arghya and rice-ball should all be done; this alone is the prescribed rule.
The ancestors are gods to the gods, and the sages to the ancestors; the gods are ancestors to the sages — by this the father prevails.
The Lord of Sacrifice is the master of ancestors, gods and men; what is given to the Lord of Sacrifice is given to all embodied beings.
A son who has a shraddha performed within the year after his father's death loses the merit earned in seven births; there is no doubt.
Ancestors who have become ghosts, their rice-ball and water rites neglected, all wander on the wind, tormented by hunger and thirst.
When the father has entered the state of a ghost, the ancestral rite lapses; but if the mother dies, the ancestral rite does not lapse.
